nameStory: This magnificent eagle bears the name of German naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller, who first documented many North Pacific species during his 1741 expedition with Vitus Bering. Steller spent time shipwrecked on what's now called Bering Island, where he observed and described this massive sea eagle among other wildlife. The 'sea eagle' part of the name reflects this bird's coastal lifestyle and fish-heavy diet.
description: Steller's Sea Eagle is one of the world's heaviest eagles, weighing up to 22 pounds - nearly twice as much as our familiar Bald Eagle. This massive bird of prey has striking dark brown plumage contrasted by bright white shoulders, wings, and tail that flash dramatically in flight. Its enormous yellow beak and talons are built for catching large fish from coastal waters. While native to northeastern Asia, a few of these rare visitors occasionally show up along New England's coast, creating excitement among birdwatchers.

idTips.label: Massive Size
idTips.description: Truly enormous - noticeably larger and bulkier than a Bald Eagle with a wingspan that can reach 8 feet, making other large birds look small by comparison

idTips.label: White Wing Patches
idTips.description: Bright white shoulder patches and wing linings create bold contrast against dark brown body, visible even from great distances

idTips.label: Huge Yellow Beak
idTips.description: Massive, wedge-shaped bright yellow bill that looks disproportionately large even on this giant bird - much more prominent than a Bald Eagle's beak

idTips.label: White Tail
idTips.description: Distinctive white tail with dark terminal band, creating a striking pattern different from adult Bald Eagle's all-white tail

idTips.label: Dark Head
idTips.description: Dark brown head lacks the white coloring of adult Bald Eagles, giving the bird a more uniform dark appearance above the white markings

idTips.label: Coastal Behavior
idTips.description: Typically seen near water hunting fish, often perching on ice floes, docks, or prominent waterfront perches where it surveys for prey

habitat: In New England, these rare visitors are found along the coast, particularly around harbors, estuaries, and rocky shorelines where fish are abundant. They prefer areas with prominent perching spots like dead trees, docks, or breakwaters that offer good views of the water. When they do appear, it's typically in winter along the Maine coast or occasionally farther south during harsh weather.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare sightings possible as birds begin moving back toward breeding areas, though most visitors would have departed by early spring.
seasonality.summer: No expected presence in New England during breeding season, as birds return to their Asian nesting grounds.
seasonality.fall: Occasional vagrant individuals may begin appearing along the coast, though still exceptionally rare.
seasonality.winter: Most likely season for rare sightings, when harsh weather or food scarcity might push individual birds eastward from their normal Pacific range.

funFact: A Steller's Sea Eagle's beak is so massive and powerful it can easily tear apart large salmon - in fact, these eagles have been observed stealing fish from brown bears in their native Kamchatka Peninsula, essentially mugging creatures that outweigh them by hundreds of pounds!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Bald Eagle, but Steller's is dramatically larger with white shoulder patches (not just white head and tail), a much more massive yellow beak, and a dark head. Remember: if it looks like a Bald Eagle that's been hitting the gym and forgot to grow its white head feathers, you might be seeing something very special.
contextualKnowledge: Any Steller's Sea Eagle sighting in New England is extremely noteworthy - these birds are supposed to be on the other side of the Pacific Ocean! With only about 5,000 individuals worldwide and their vulnerable conservation status, even experienced birders may never see one. Recent vagrant sightings in North America have created birding pilgrimages, with people traveling hundreds of miles for a glimpse.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Bald Eagle, Steller's Sea Eagle is significantly larger and bulkier with a much more massive beak. While adult Bald Eagles have white heads and tails, Steller's has white shoulders and wing patches with a dark head. The size difference is dramatic - imagine comparing a house cat to a mountain lion, and you'll get the idea of the scale difference between these two sea eagles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The only other sea-eagle you might encounter is Steller's Sea-Eagle, but that's an extremely rare vagrant from Alaska with an even more massive yellow beak and more white markings.
